sources.name: Eleanor Rivera
sources.quote: You know, at 12th Street, we see how everything outside the station affects what happens inside. Fog, holidays, even a big game downtown - it all changes the flow. People adjust their routines, and we adjust right along with them. It's not just about numbers going up or down - it's about reading the neighborhood's rhythm and keeping things moving.

sources.name: Coen Cartier
sources.quote: Lately at 12th Street, I've noticed the crowds come and go with what's happening around town. When there's a game or some big vote at City Hall, we get that rush before and after. Other days, especially with the fog rolling in, folks seem to stay put more. It's not just one thing - it's how all these pieces fit together that changes who's waiting at the curb when I pull up.

sources.name: Joel Wren
sources.quote: You know, I've been seeing more folks hopping on the buses lately—especially down at 12th Street. It's good to see people out and about, trusting the system again. But what really gets me is the crew keeping those buses running. Those mechanics and drivers? They're the ones putting in the long hours to make sure everyone gets where they need to go, rain or shine, game day or not.

sources.name: Jerald Jensen
sources.quote: You want to know about 12th Street Station? I'll tell you—when the fog rolls in thick like it did last week, or when there's some big game downtown, I see it in the trash cans. Overflowing. More coffee cups, more wrappers, more people rushing through like the place owes them money. And when the Baylight vote happened? Whole different kind of crowd—folks in suits leaving flyers everywhere, talking loud like they own the benches I just cleaned. Ridership numbers? I don't know numbers. But I know my mop water gets dirtier faster when the city's got something brewing.

approvedQuotes.text: You know, at 12th Street, we see how everything outside the station affects what happens inside. Fog, holidays, even a big game downtown - it all changes the flow. People adjust their routines, and we adjust right along with them. It's not just about numbers going up or down - it's about reading the neighborhood's rhythm and keeping things moving.

Lately at 12th Street, I've noticed the crowds come and go with what's happening around town. When there's a game or some big vote at City Hall, we get that rush before and after. Other days, especially with the fog rolling in, folks seem to stay put more. It's not just one thing - it's how all these pieces fit together that changes who's waiting at the curb when I pull up.

You know, I've been seeing more folks hopping on the buses lately—especially down at 12th Street. It's good to see people out and about, trusting the system again. But what really gets me is the crew keeping those buses running. Those mechanics and drivers? They're the ones putting in the long hours to make sure everyone gets where they need to go, rain or shine, game day or not.

You want to know about 12th Street Station? I'll tell you—when the fog rolls in thick like it did last week, or when there's some big game downtown, I see it in the trash cans. Overflowing. More coffee cups, more wrappers, more people rushing through like the place owes them money. And when the Baylight vote happened? Whole different kind of crowd—folks in suits leaving flyers everywhere, talking loud like they own the benches I just cleaned. Ridership numbers? I don't know numbers. But I know my mop water gets dirtier faster when the city's got something brewing.
